10.0.s.en: 1. The first woe against the leaders:

10.0.0.en: 1 Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and to the scribes that write grievousness which they have prescribed; 2 To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless! 3 And what will ye do in the day of visitation, when the desolation shall come from far? To whom will ye flee for help? And where will ye leave your glory? 4 They shall either bow down among the prisoners, or fall under the slain. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

10.0.1.en: Some see the woe directed here against the leaders as a continuation of what was said in the previous chapter about the pride of Israel, and they prove this by the fact that it also ends with the phrase that was repeated before: "For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still" (Isa 9:12, 17, 21; 10:4). On this view the discourse is directed against the leaders of the ten tribes (Israel). However, the rest of the discourse is addressed to Jerusalem, the capital of Judah, and for this reason some scholars hold that what is said here applies to the leaders of both kingdoms, since they were alike in evil.

10.0.2.en: God exposes the unjust conduct of the leaders, which centers on judging falsely and ruling with injustice [1]. They keep the weak from enjoying their stolen rights, and they rob the poor of their right, especially the fatherless and the widows [2]. As the Wise Man says: "So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power" (Eccl 4:1).

10.0.3.en: Now, since Isaiah perceives the justice of God, especially in His defense of the weak, he asks these leaders:

10.1.0.en: "And what will ye do in the day of visitation, when the desolation shall come from far? To whom will ye flee for help? And where will ye leave your glory? They shall either bow down among the prisoners, or fall under the slain" [3-4]. Punishment is certainly coming, especially upon the religious and civil leaders; this is a settled matter and a truth that cannot be ignored. As he said before: "Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him" (Isa 3:11). They will find no help, because what helps us in judgment is our mercy and compassion toward others. Their glories vanish because these were bound to time and not to God. Therefore some of them fall as captives, to bow down in humiliation among the prisoners, and some are killed when Assyria attacks them, and so fall under the bodies of others. They trampled the right of the weak, and so others tread them under their feet.

10.2.0.en: Yet for all this God still stretches out the hand of His love to save them from their evil: "For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still" [4].

10.3.0.en: 5 "Woe to Assyria, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation. 6 I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. 7 Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few. 8 For he saith, Are not my princes altogether kings? 9 Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus? 10 As my hand hath found the kingdoms of the idols, and their graven images did excel them of Jerusalem and of Samaria; 11 Shall I not, as I have done unto Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols?" 12 Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks. 13 For he saith, "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the kings like a valiant man: 14 And my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs that are left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped." 15 Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up him that is not wood. 16 Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory he shall kindle a burning like the burning of a fire. 17 And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; 18 And shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body: and it shall be as when a sick man melts away. 19 And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few, that a child may write them.

10.3.1.en: The prophet has already spoken of Assyria's military power, its might and its victory even over the people of God. He has also affirmed that what befell the people came by divine permission for discipline. But Assyria exalted itself against God and reckoned that by this victory it had conquered the God of this people and humbled Him... Therefore the Lord turns back and disciplines Assyria itself, so haughty and arrogant.

10.3.2.en: The prophet Isaiah was accustomed to speak boldly and frankly. While he calls Assyria the rod of God's anger, and the staff in their hand the indignation of the Lord [5], because Assyria is an instrument for carrying out the Lord's discipline, we find him calling the people of God "an hypocritical nation" and "the people of my wrath" [6], because this people carried the outward form of worship while corruption crept into their inner life. This is what led him to call the people by hateful names and to declare that God delivers them over to Assyria for plunder and spoil, so that Assyria may tread them under foot and they become trodden down like the mire of the streets... Whoever makes light of the holy life in the Lord hands his life over to corruption and ruin, and collapses, so that the enemy of good mocks him and treads him under his feet.

10.4.0.en: Assyria did not realize this truth, that it was merely an instrument of discipline [7]; rather, in pride it said: "Are not my princes altogether kings?" [8]. That is, the governors whom the king of Assyria appoints under his command are all kings, so what then is his own position? He is the king of kings!

10.5.0.en: He also said: "Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?" [9]. Scholars hold that the speaker here is Sennacherib the Assyrian, boasting of his victories together with those of Sargon before him, as victories won on behalf of Assyria as a whole, which show the futility of resisting the Assyrian advance.

10.5.1.en: Perhaps by Calno is meant "Calneh," mentioned with Hamath and Gath in (Amos 6:2), which is thought to be Kullani or the modern Kulanhu, six miles from Arpad, near Aleppo.

10.5.2.en: Carchemish: the eastern capital of the Hittites, west of the Euphrates at a ford in the river and north of where it meets the Sajur. Its location was excellent for trade, and it was very rich. Ashurnasirpal of Assyria (885-860 B.C.) exacted a very large tribute from it, and Sargon captured it in 717 B.C., and with its fall the Hittite empire fell. The Romans called it Circesium; on its site now stands Jarablus.

10.5.3.en: Arpad: a city in Aram about 13 miles north of Hamath, now on the site called "Tell Arpad." The Assyrians captured it in the ninth century before Christ, but it rebelled against them, and they returned and captured it several times, boasting of their victory over it.

10.6.0.en: Thus the greatest cities of the Hittites or the Arameans did not stand before Assyria; will the cities of Judah and Israel stand before it? Assyria reckoned that it had conquered the gods of the nations and the idols that protect them, so that the God of Israel or of Judah would not stand before it either [10-11], supposing that He is on the same level as these idols.

10.7.0.en: God allowed it this much, but He turns back and disciplines Assyria for its scorn of Him: "Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks. For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the kings like a valiant man: and my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs that are left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped" [13-14].

10.7.1.en: Thus Assyria supposed that by its own strength and wisdom it had done mighty works: it ruled kings and removed peoples, destroyed, killed and grew rich. In its campaigns it looked upon the peoples as the nest of a bird, with no strength or power, and plundered the abandoned eggs in it... No one was found to stand before it or to utter a word.

10.7.2.en: Assyria did not realize that it was an axe or a saw that God used for discipline, and so the instrument exalted itself over the one who wields it. Therefore God disciplines it in this way:

10.8.0.en: A. He sends leanness among "his fat ones," that is, the mighty heroes of his army [16].

10.8.1.en: B. He kindles under "his glory," that is, his army, a burning like the burning of a fire [16], and it consumes it until it becomes ashes. God becomes "the light of Israel" into a fire that devours Assyria, and the Holy One a flame that crushes the enemy [17]. In other words, God, who is light for the believers and the mystery of sanctification of their life, becomes a devouring fire and a flame for the wicked who resist Him.

10.9.0.en: C. He destroys his army so that a small number remains (the trees of the forest), whose names a child can write [19]. This is as regards number; as regards strength, they lose their spiritual and bodily energy and become like a consumptive who melts away [18].

10.10.0.en: 20 And it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob, shall no more again stay upon him that smote them; but shall stay upon the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. 21 The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God. 22 For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness. 23 For the Lord GOD of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land.

10.11.0.en: The prophets often spoke of the "remnant" that will be saved. By it they meant the very few who remain faithful to the Lord amid the collapse of the religious leaders and the corruption of the judges, the rulers and the people as well. This remnant, which escapes the corruption of the community and its abominations, is saved from the great tribulation in the time of bitter trial (Rev 3:10). This remnant that escapes the oppression of Assyria does not rejoice in its return to Jerusalem, but in something greater: it rejoices in its meeting with the mighty God Himself [21].

10.11.1.en: The Apostle Paul quoted the saying of the prophet Isaiah [(Isa 22-23) LXX], saying: "Isaiah also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved: for he is finishing the matter and judging in righteousness, because the Lord will make a decreed matter upon the earth" (Rom 9:27-28).

10.11.2.en: This saying occurs in Isaiah [(Isa 22-23) LXX] and carried a prophecy about the captives, since they were very many in comparison with the very few who escape from captivity... and that God allowed this, and even decreed this discipline for the sake of righteousness. The Apostle applied this prophecy more broadly to the Messianic age, when a very great number of the Jews are held captive in unbelief, refusing to believe in the Messiah, while few are saved by accepting the Messiah the Savior; and God allowed this for the sake of righteousness, to open the door to the Gentiles.

10.11.3.en: St. John Chrysostom comments: [He means that I do not care about the multitude (the huge number), and I am not swayed by the race (the Jews), but I save those who come forward as worthy of salvation. He did not mention "the sand of the sea" for no reason, but to remind them of the ancient promise (Gen 22:17; 32:12), which they had made themselves unworthy of. Why then are you troubled if the promise is not fulfilled (for all), since all the prophets showed that not everyone is saved? Then the Apostle also shows the way of salvation... "For he is finishing the matter and judging (quickly) in righteousness, because the Lord will make a decreed matter (quickly) upon the earth" (Rom 9:28)... This matter is faith, which carries salvation in few words: "That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved" (Rom 10:9). Behold, you see that the Lord is completing a short word upon the earth, and the wonder is that this short word carries not salvation only but righteousness as well.] He also says: [Lest you think that God cares only for the huge number, he says: "Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved."] And St. Augustine says: [This is the remnant of that nation which believes in Christ.]

10.12.s.en: 4. Be not afraid, O my people:

10.12.0.en: 24 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, "O my people that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian: he shall smite thee with a rod, and shall lift up his staff against thee, after the manner of Egypt. 25 For yet a very little while, and the indignation shall cease, and mine anger in their destruction." 26 And the LORD of hosts shall stir up a scourge for him according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb: and as his rod was upon the sea, so shall he lift it up after the manner of Egypt. 27 And it shall come to pass in that day, that his burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck, and the yoke shall be destroyed because of the fatness.

10.12.1.en: Some scholars hold that the prophecy here points to the following event: when Hezekiah the son of Ahaz and his successor refused to pay tribute, Sennacherib the Assyrian attacked Judah with a strong army and besieged Jerusalem, and was on the point of taking the city, but God ordered its deliverance. The army was slain and Sennacherib fled, where his sons killed him.

10.12.2.en: The prophecy here pointed to an important matter, namely that God is the One who works in all generations. God does not cease to command His people not to fear, for He is the Father who is committed to our life, our salvation, our growth and our peace, and He works in every age with an uplifted arm for the salvation of His believers. If the exodus of the children of Israel, or their deliverance from slavery, is counted an extraordinary thing that reveals God's care for His believers, then in the days of Hezekiah He repeats their exodus or deliverance on a mightier level, amid the bitterness that all were suffering.

10.13.0.en: God asks His people not to fear Assyria, for it will be destroyed, as God raises up a scourge against it [26]. He strikes it with His angel with a deadly blow (2 Chr 32:21), as He struck Oreb, the prince of Midian, before (Judg 7:25; Ps 83:11), and as He struck Pharaoh and his hosts in the Red Sea through the rod of Moses [26]. Thus God destroys Assyria to remove this yoke from the shoulder of His people [27] and from their neck because of the fatness (the oil), for the sake of the holy anointing which King David received, and his sons after him.

10.13.1.en: The second matter is that the Anointed One, the mighty Messiah, grants rest to the whole earth, and peace, through His blessed reign... This is the main line of the whole book, indeed of the Holy Bible in both Testaments.

10.14.0.en: 28 He is come to Aiath, he is passed to Migron; at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages: 29 They are gone over the passage: they have taken up their lodging at Geba; Ramah is afraid; Gibeah of Saul is fled. 30 Lift up thy voice, O daughter of Gallim: hearken, O Laishah: poor Anathoth! 31 Madmenah is removed; the inhabitants of Gebim gather themselves to flee. 32 As yet shall he remain at Nob that day: he shall shake his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.

10.14.1.en: Before speaking of the fall of Assyria, the prophet spoke of the Assyrian invasion of Judah, to make clear its mighty military ability and the speed of its advance toward Jerusalem the capital, with the weakness of Judah's resistance, indeed its absence, and how Judah was terrified and trembled [28-32]. The prophet gave a poetic description that reveals the bitterness of the cities of Judah, but Assyria halts at Nob (a city of the priests lying north of Jerusalem), perhaps to rest the army and prepare to confront Jerusalem. Sennacherib stood there to raise his hand and stretch it out in threat against Jerusalem [32], and so appeared as a lofty, arrogant tree. He threatened to crush Jerusalem and did not realize that God had allowed his own crushing, and that He would strip from him the branches with which he exalts himself.

10.14.2.en: In this prophecy God does not mean Sennacherib alone, but every evil movement that resists the Church of God or any of His children.

10.15.0.en: 33 Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled. 34 And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one.

10.15.1.en: God proclaims the complete destruction of Assyria, for He lops its branches and even pulls up its roots, so that its loftiness collapses and its glory comes down to the dust [33-34]. This is the fruit of pride!
